review_text_raw:
This is gonna be a lengthy review. I'll add a TL;DR at the bottom.

When I first went to view the page for this game, there were many questions that began flooding my mind. And now that I've played the game almost to its entirety, I think that I can answer most of these questions that interested consumers passing by may have. This game was a real treat, and I think that it deserves more attention than it's received.


[h1] Is Hacknet realistic? [/h1]

If you mean "realistic" as in "Is this game close to hacking in real life?" then the answer is no. This game is not realistic because it is fun and doesn't make you paranoid. You are in possession of a bunch of hacking tools that put up the kinds of graphics you'd expect to be running on computers in a 90's hacker film, and the way these tools work is by executing them and waiting for the flashy hacking graphics to stop flashing so that you can run another flashy hacker tool until you gain administrative system access. Granted, it's more complex than that, which is why this game is really enjoyable, but you're not going to be writing complex algorithms to overload proxy servers and bypass tracing measures. That's what the 90's tools are for.

That being said, this may be as close as gaming will ever come to realistic hacking. Because anything that tries to be precicely like real hacking that doesn't give you fancy hacker programs probably isn't going to be a very fun game. And this, again, is a fun game. The entire game takes place on a computer's operating system, and every hack you perform is done through this system. In addition, the commands you use are based on real UNIX commands, even if the commands are typically used to activate the previously-mentioned hacking programs. It's certainly more realistic than games where you push a button and your character goes [i]"I'm in" [/i] like Watch_Dogs and Quadrilateral Cowboy (That isn't to say that they're bad games, just that they're not trying to be realistic hacking simulations which, again, isn't necessarily a bad thing).


[h1] Is this game immersive? Will I feel like a hacker even if I'm not performing real hacks? [/h1]

Oh, yes. If you want to feel like the genius hacker that always appears in Hollywood films but rarely gets any time for actual character development, then this game is for you. The presentation of this game is great, and it really helps to sell that feeling of accomplishment that you get when you pull off a successful job. After about 30 minutes in, I had to re-check the steam store to make sure that I wasn't accessing a multiplayer hacking simulator. But nope, I was even able to play this game in airplane mode. As the store page mentions, there are very few things that break the immersion by being obvious parts of a video game. To complete a job, you email the client explaining that you've finished. To acquire a new tool, you have to copy said tool to your home computer from its rightful owner. 

And this immersive presentation goes a long way in the overall experience. I know that not everybody responds the same way, but I found certain parts to incite genuine emotion in a way that few other games have managed to pull off. Like when you're given the option to accept a job in which [spoiler]you have to euthanize a dying man by hacking his pacemaker [/spoiler], or when [spoiler]you run "OpenCDtray" on your own system and your real computer's disc tray opens and may potentially scare the hell out of you[/spoiler]. So even if you're using overpowered tools to open systems that nobody bothers to check, you'll probably still feel really good doing so.


[h1] Do I need to know coding or hacking in order to understand this game? [/h1]

No, you don't. The tutorial explains everything pretty well, and it makes sure that you understand how the systems work before even thinking about letting you out into the hacking world. No coding is required (I'm not even sure if coding algorithms is possible with the interface), and most of the game's difficulty comes with memorizing the commands and executing them at the appropriate times. That being said, if you don't know a whole lot about computers, the most difficult task will probably be [spoiler] getting your interface back after being locked to terminal mode by another hacker [/spoiler]. But if you experiment enough, then you'll ususally find the solutions to most of the challenges, and there are plenty of walkthroughs and tips out there if you end up getting desperate. But I was able to finish the game with little prior programming experience. If you know how to navigate a computer's interface or have downloaded and fixed mods on to other games, then you'll probably be fine with this game. Just, you know, don't delete important files or screw up on a trace aversion. I don't know if this game prevents you from screwing yourself over, and everybody's too scared to find out.


[h1] Is the game worth ten bucks? [/h1]

Yeah, I'd say so. You'll probably get around 10 hours out of it if you're doing the main story without any outside assitance, 14-15 hours if you're also doing the labrynths DLC. I'd say that it's not everybody's cup of tea; surely, your relative who spends all day exclusively playing [i] Fortnite [/i] would probably get turned off by this, but odds are you're at least mildly interested in this game if you're reading this review right now, considering that this game gets talked about as much as what brand of toilet paper you prefer when you're finished up on the toilet. So yeah, I'd recommend this game to anybody reading this review.


[h1] Oh, boy. It's one of those games that tries to sell its soundtrack as DLC. Is it good enough to warrant a purchase? [/h1]

I was honestly surprised by this game's soundtrack. Again, I understand that everybody has different tastes in music, but I found this particular OST track good to write and do homework to. It felt really good to listen to in-game while hacking servers and computers. The music is used as sort of an indicator on what part of the game you're currently at, and when the song changes, you know you're probably making progress. I found that [spoiler] Roller Mobster by Carpenter Brut [/spoiler] fit this game better than it did for HM2. That being said, I haven't purchased the soundtrack since most of it is available on YouTube anyways. And yes, it's ten dollars. Fifteen dollars for the main game and DLC soundtrack. So while I'll admit that the soundtrack is pretty good, I'd only spend the extra fifteen bucks if you like having the songs directly at your fingertips at all times.


[h1] TL;DR [/h1]

This is a great game that may be as close to realistic hacking as gaming will come while still remaining enjoyable. The presentation and aeshetic really add a lot to it, and you don't need to be experienced with programming or hacking in order to complete it. It's worth the money and gives around 10 hours of playtime assuming you don't mess up massively and have to start a new game. I'm gonna give this a thumbs up, and I wish it came out later so that I could put it in my favorite 2018 games list.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very unique genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. [/h1]

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc.

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it.

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into.

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into.

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look around some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

I feel slightly bad giving this game a negative review given that I enjoyed most of the time I spent playing it, but I honestly can't recommend it.

The positives are more than adequately covered in other reviews, but for completeness: It does a solid job of recreating the Hollywood hacker fantasy, with hacks and counter-hacks, proxies, firewalls, trace countdowns, and all that good stuff. The story is nicely paced, with plenty of humour and knowing pop-culture references as you move from small-time nuisance hacks to big-time corporate takedowns. And there is a mildly satisfying payoff when you figure out the occasional less-than-straightforward mission or discover a new mechanic.

Therein lies one of the major problems for me, though. For the most part the missions are fairly routine and don't really require any genuine creativity or problem-solving. You are pretty much handed the tools you need as you need them, and for each obstacle you need to overcome there will be a single tool for the job. As an example: the procedure for bypassing a firewall is to repeatedly type the 'analyze' command until you get the solution, and then to type in that solution - once you have done that once, it is entirely routine. I rarely felt clever solving the missions, and for a game like this I consider that a major failing.

As another reviewer pointed out, there are also elements of the game that seem to be either completely superficial or just unfinished. The best example is the scrubbing of logs, which is quite laborious, but presented at the beginning of the game as a vital measure to cover your tracks. So, the player diligently does so, until inevitably one time they forget, and then DUN DUN DUN...nothing. Apparently this feature is better implemented in the DLC extensions, but I didn't get that far.

Finally, the aspect of the game that ultimately ruined it for me: it is possible to irrevocably break your save game and have no way to recover. If you accidentally delete a file that is mission-critical to the main storyline, and don't notice until the next auto-save (or you save the game yourself), it's game over. This happened to me at about the 4.5 hour mark, and while it certainly wouldn't have taken me that long to get back to the same point from scratch, the game just doesn't work as a rogue-like - I would be going through exactly the same fiddly steps to complete exactly the same routine missions, and I just couldn't face it.

If you want to play a hacking game with a similar aesthetic but some genuine code-based problem-solving, I'd strongly recommend EXAPUNKS, or for an absolutely brilliant command-prompt-based-rogue-like try Duskers.

review_text_raw:
Cheap and easy adventure game, but not really a puzzle game. 

The game is fun for what it is, but it isn't what I expected at all. When I fired it up I thought it was going to be a much deeper experience. That isn't to say it wasn't enjoyable, it at the very minimum had some amazing atmosphere and music. It was fun for a bit to read through old IRC chat logs and relive its heyday. 

Most of the game is following instructions without question. This was never subverted, and everything was as simple as expected throughout the entire game. I was expecting a few missions where I edited records, or deleted files, to backfire, and I would have to restore those records or find another copy of the file, but nothing of the sort happened. I instead became super hackerman within 2 hours and with some software I downloaded I was able to break into just about every computer on the planet. The game in general isn't particularly hard, and if you know anything about unix commands, you can get through everything fairly quickly. If you lose or someone traces you the worst that happens is you reboot your virtual computer, and the most you lose out is some time but that is about it, so the stakes are about as low as possible. 

There were a few bugs, and few missions never triggered unless I followed a guide. That is the only reason I have 8 hours on the game, I beat it easily doing just about everything except the DLC in around 4 hours. It took me redoing a particular part twice to get the /el message board missions to trigger but if you ignore 100% completion read quickly, know your unix commands and stick to the main story, you can finish even faster.

I do have a few gripes though, for one the user tags at the moment say it is a simulation and programming game. However this can't be further from the truth. The tutorial at first used real unix commands to control your computer, and I was preparing for a much more "hardcore experience". However, the more that I played the more that I was disappointed with the puzzles. It took me until about an hour in before I realized it isn't a puzzle game at all. It really just an adventure game. Very few locks have time pressure and that is the hardest part of the game. Otherwise you just follow instructions and don't really think about what is going on.  The simulation aspects are fairly shallow, and at most the "hacking" is just run multiple programs, one after another. There is no programming at all, and I have no idea how why that is a tag. I think that some people misinterpret the terminal as programming. The terminal is something most people used to interact with computers up until the late 90s, and if you use Linux, you use it pretty much every day. Its just an alternate interface, it would be like calling using a mouse programming.

Pick it up on a deep sale if you want to kill some time, but there are other games that are much deeper and have more going on. The atmosphere is nice, and snooping through old IRC logs is worth the nostalgia alone, but if you have no interest in that, I would recommend for you to pass on this.

review_text_raw:
Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

review_text_raw:
Good: 
[list]
    [*]the command line UI is accurate, and makes you feel a lot like a real hacker.
    [*]nice music
    [*]lots of little easter eggs
    [*]technically very accurate (uses correct port numbers, IP addresses, and more)
[/list]

Bad: 
[list]
   [*]core gameplay is extremely repetitive and time consuming (which is an awful combination)
[/list]

The core gameplay of Hacknet revolves around you, a hacker, who can run several different programs to hack into a server and complete some task for a client. For example, hacking into the fried chicken chain CFC server and stealing the list of 11 secret herbs and spices.

It's an interesting concept to start with, however the game falls extremely short in that the gameplay never evolves into anything that is challenging or involves meaningful decision making. 

Hacking each server in the entire game is exactly the same. That is no exaggeration. You literally do the exact same 3-7 things for each server you encounter in order to hack into it. And the worst part about this process is that the "hacking" requires no user interaction. You simply wait 1-2 minutes for the hacking programs to finish, and then you complete whatever task you were assigned to do on the server.

At no point do you need to make any in game decisions when hacking. At no point do you have any decision to make that can affect the gameplay. And that's really where it all falls apart for me. What am I really doing in this game? Because the game really lacks in the feeling of accomplishment.

I can completely understand how this gameplay can appeal to people who want to feel like a hacker, because the game definitely hits the mark in that regard. But once you get past that, you realise there is very little "gameplay" to be had. It just feels like a demo.

Shall..we..play..a..game?

Welcome to Hacknet, a game that made me feel so much that i was somewhere inside a 80's hacker movie it had me waiting for Joshua to call me to tell me we needed to finish the game we started.

I was really surprised at how much i enjoyed the game being that it is mostly text based but to the details.

The game is niche but even if you have only the most basic and i mean BASIC keyboarding skills you can quickly get the commands down. If you've ever set up your own linux box and just messed around with it a little bit you can play this game. If you watched Wargames, Hackers, Ghost in the Shell, or played Cyberpunk, Shadowrun, or Anarchy Online you will want to play this game. I picked it up during a 75% off sale and only now started playing and it is very addicting and hilarious at the same time. There are some parts that really screw with your mind and so as not to spoil the story let me just say that you must "role play" the persona in the game. When the things that screw with your mind happen you have to ask yourself "What would my "Hacker" persona do?"

The soundtrack is very techno-club and adds to the overall feel of the game nicely.
The learning curve is a bit like a roller coaster and if you aren't paying attention you can find yourself stuck and wondering what to do.

You won't learn to code, or "hack", or script anything. You will get really good practice at some few basic Linux commands in the terminal which is good practice and fun. I haven't found a binary compiler in the game so haven't been able to figure out what the binary code files are or if i'm even supposed to figure out what they are. but it's still fun to wonder.

This game has great multi-player potential but other reviews indicate that the developers may not do any more with it. Also there is no multi-monitor support which would be a really nice touch but isn't likely to happen either.

I've put almost 5 hours at this point; found a bunch of stuff; lost a bunch of stuff; got my stuff back and loved every minute of it. The game won't teach you to be a hacker, but it is the Hacking game you didn't know that you desperately needed to play.

It is a niche game to be sure but if you are feeling a bit nostalgic after the gaming references i've made, download the game and enjoy. I did buy it on very cheap sale, 75% off,  but $10 isn't an excessive price point for a really fun game. I don't see a whole lot of replaying the game due to the linear storyline. Steam community has added some content and there seems to be enough material from the community to make the game worthwhile.

help
help 2
help 3

The ability to move forward in the game is usually found in those tools. If you are stuck, study the "help" pages.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is an absolute gem of a game. 

[b]TLDR: [/b]While people already familiar with using *nix or general programing principles may find this game not too deep or challenging, it offers a well thought out narrative, with fun game mechanics and excels at teaching you about computer essentials without you even realizing it. 


[b]More thoughts:[/b] 

While this game isn't perfect, I would still reccomend it to anyone who has even a remote interest in computers. Even if you only want to feel like a hacker in a movie, that game gives you that feeling. If you want to learn more about the general concepts of computer-, program-, and network-architecture, this game is a great launching-point, before you start reading more "serious" or conventional literature on the subject. 

Now, the mechanics are pretty straight-forward. You gain various programs through completing quests, which, in turn, can be used to bypass more complex security. You also gain the ability to run commands through other computers, allowing you, for example, to pretty much emulate a DDOS attack. Timing is also important, so be ready to type "dc" + [enter] if you're being tracked. AAAAAAAAANNNNNNDDDDDD............

.....
.....
.....

that's pretty much it when it comes to mechanics. The rest is working your way through systems full of mostly text-files, a lot of them taken from bash.org (hilarious quotes from internet chats, NSFW, but great!), and a lot of fun easter-eggs for nerds and fans of "hacker-culture" as it has been created by Hollywood. There even are multiple references to the movie "Hackers", a must see in my opinion. ;)

Now, the mechanics got old after not too long (a good 8 hours), mainly due to you unlocking a lot of the tools that you need pretty quickly. I'll talk more about overall gameplay features in just a moment. 

The narrative is fun, well paced, and interwoven well with the gameplay mechanics. I won't spoil anything, just watch the trailer and you get the general premise. 

The overall game is simplified, to allow people without prior experience to enjoy it, but encourages experimentation and exploration of what you can do, giving you plenty of examples and hints along the way to teach you, without you even realizing it, a lot about how your system works. Absolutely amazing!

Concerning the lack of gameplay features, the dev is amazing. Yup, one dev. And he's already said that he wants to implement multiplayer. If that happens, this will become one of the best games out there. Period. Plus he wants to continue to push content for the game. Not to mention, that the community as a whole is awesome and really suportive for newcomers. 

In its current state, it's well worth the price its asking for. As the dev continues to push more content, the game will continue to expand and improve. 

Please support this game, as its honestly trying to be different and fun, without a lot of the backstabbing and abusive tactics emplyed by all too many triple AAA studios/publishers. I can guarantee, you'll have a blast playing this!

Edit 2016: what I've said before still applies. I would just like to point towards the roadmap the dev has for 2016, which includes multiplayer and steam-workshop integration for custom missions throughout various points this year. http://steamcommunity.com/games/365450/announcements/detail/955130645658936382 

****DISCLAIMER:****
 WIll not actually refund any purchases if you are somehow not pleased with the overall game. 
Mouse and Mechanical Keyboard sold seperatly.
Batteries not included.

How would hacking be without knowledge, skills or creativity? 

The same "hacks" get applied repetitively to open ports and then read/download/delete files over and over again. I've seen more challenging escape rooms.

Don't get me wrong - It's amazing for an indie game developed by one person. But on the other hand there are CTFs with a nice story out there that keep me busy without making me feel like in a hamster wheel. If you are into cyber security, don't waste your time with this. 

But if you have zero knowledge and want to feel like a hacker, this game teaches a few basics about handling a Linux-like OS (with wine for .exe files) and simulates how to move through a network.

It would be great to focus on only a few stories and individualize the targets instead of seeing generic ancient bash content on every PC. Also I missed a proper C2 setup with own proxies that I can create, privilege escalation and lateral movement instead of being admin immediately, alternating attack vectors and the option to create scripts or at least files ("touch") and directories ("mkdir"). This would have been a nice starting point to start playing around, break things out of curiosity and discover the possibilities instead of moving inside the box all the time.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet... I don't even know where to start with this game.

Hacknet is not your average game. Some games may be incredibly immersive, like FPSes and VR games. Hacknet is not designed to be like this.

In most cases, Hacknet is also not an intense game. You aren't tested on your reaction time or click speed. You are tested, instead, on your abilities to adapt to different environments and solve problems as they pop up in your face.

Hacknet is also not what I'd consider a Christian game. Although there are few swear words to be found in the game (minus the IRC logs), Hacknet's plot involves learning to be a hacker using a simplistic set of Unix-inspired tools and a combination of a GUI and terminal environment.

When you start the game, you may not be incredibly impressed with the low amount of character development, as the basis of the game is just learning to use your environment, but you will eventually learn that a repetitive element of the game becomes a major part of the plot.

Even as shown by the creator's development timelapse (available to view at the end of the game), this game is not incredibly complex, but hours upon hours of work have been put into it and the average gamer will gain hours of fun.

To summarize the game as a whole, Hacknet is about diving into a world that is not your own and helping to fulfill an uncannily skilled hacker's death wishes. You learn to take advantage of a user environment known as the Hacknet OS and join several virtual hacker groups in an attempt to follow breadcrumbs left behind by Bit.

The soundtrack is co-written by several somewhat popular artists. It is dynamic to your actions in the game, having more intense music being played in more intense missions, and likewise for calmer, more reflective portions of the game. (If you loved the soundtrack as much as I did, please be sure to purchase it as DLC. It's available in the game folder after purchasing and downloading. My favorite tracks are Broken Boy and Bit.)

I am not a game critic, simply a lowly gamer. But the impact this game has had on my life is incredible. The plot is masterfully crafted and better than any movie I've ever watched. The graphics, although simple, are fancy enough to fit the experience (although epileptic persons may want to avoid the end of the game). As I have described, the soundtrack is amazing. Everything about this game makes it worth at least a couple hours away from Fortnite.

11/10

review_text_raw:
A highly immersive game given how graphically simple it is: basically just a bunch of text and menus. The world-building makes you really feel like a hacker being hired by various people to do all sorts of tasks. I enjoyed the game more than a lot of far more visually impressive games.

I must stress that the 'hacking' part is vastly simplified. It barely touches the basics of hacking, so don't expect the game to teach you how to hack in real-life, though it might just inspire you to learn it properly yourself. The technical aspect of the gameplay also starts to get repetitive once you've tried out all the commands and programs available to you, somewhere around the half-way point. However, the real thrill and challenge of the game lies in digging up useful information and files in the various devices you hack into, analyse them and then figure out how you can use them in order to accomplish your goal. In a sense, this feels like a hacking-themed detective game. There's also a story to the game that really picks up near the end, though some might find it a bit vague at parts.

While I thoroughly enjoyed the game from start to finish, I have to say that this game isn't for everyone. First of all, you gotta be prepared to read a lot. You don't have to read all the text, as many of the text files are purely comedic in nature, having nothing to do with accomplishing the task at hand and are just there to entertain you, but on the other hand, there are a lot of them that contain vital information towards completing your task, even if you don't realise it at first. You definitely need to be patient and observant if you want to beat the game on your own, as well as having good deductive skills to put the information you find to good use. The game does make you think a bit, though not to the extent of typical puzzle games. There are also educational text files that teach you how the various commands and programs in the game work. If you enjoy reading, then I'm sure you would enjoy this game, though there are a few typos here and there that can be annoying.

As for the gameplay, when you're not reading stuff, you're pretty much just typing away commands on your keyboard or just clicking buttons that appear on screen on the UI with your mouse. You don't have to type out everything in full, as you can use the Tab key to auto-complete commands and file names, but it does help to have good typing skills, especially as there are quite a few timed challenges in the game.

All in all, Hacknet does a great job as a hacking simulator game, making you feel like an actual hacker while still being fun to play, even if the hacking aspect is significantly dumbed-down. I recommend this game to those who wish to experience what it's like to be one of those hackers you often see in movies without having to deal with the high technical difficulty of actual hacking. Experienced hackers might find it too simple to be enjoyable, though.

review_text_raw:
Let's face it guys and girls: Most of us will never hack the headquarter of a huge and powerful concern. Most of us are actually screwed when we forget the PIN for our smartphone. And thats ok. Nothing to feel bad for.
But still....those classic hacker movies. And this Mr. Robot show. That looks so awesome. But are we interested in dedicating our freetime for our new and perhaps fleeting passion? Learn to program and hack and learn code and whatever. Books! Math! Boring stuff!
Thank God there is Hacknet, a hacking sim reminiscent of the classic game Uplink. And in a good way!

Basically, you are a hacker and you follow a storyline and/or your own ideas and hack your way through files, computer systems, security and whatnot. And, like in real life, the protagonist (you!) sits in front of the computer and does all this incredible hacking stuff from his or her chair. And in a game like this, its about the small things it does: You can click on a computer to connect with it. Or you use command codes and an IP adress. You can look through files with clicking on a button. Or you use, you guessed it, command codes to look through it. The latter feels more authentic, and sometimes, thats what you want. Actually, in my humble opinion, this game is best when you try to use as many written commands as possible. It gives you the feeling to be a real hacker. 

In many games, hacking is an afterthought. A minigame at best. Like in Deus Ex: Hacking belongs to Cyberpunk like awesome armblades, but it is basically connect-the-dots with a nicer color palette. And thats totally cool, cause you dont want to obstruct the core gameplay.
But if you want to feel like a real hacker, disrupting the system chilling in a comfy chair, then look no further than Hacknet. Choose your nickname, learn a few basic commands that the game teaches you and discover your inner anarchist. The game gets more complicated along the way and you have to think a bit more, but thats what you want. Hacking the computer of a smalltown retirement home is one thing, but getting these corporations: Thats the holy grail of cyberpunk-esque hacking, isnt it?

Weird long review - short message: Are you into hacking simulators? Wont get much better than this game.

An absolutely engaging and wonderful game. This is one of those gems that lingers in your library for a while ominously taunting you. I'm going to break this review up in a few sections. The game lets you explore what it's like to be a hacker. Well more of a stereotypical movie meme hacker, but still that's a perk here. You should expect to be snooping into people's computers, reading their emails, and finding all of their dirty secrets. With that in mind this game plays more like an information-gathering puzzle simulator.

1. Gameplay
This may be the biggest "fear" new players may have after viewing the trailer. This game involves typing out commands in a terminal, but really it's just similar to a "text based" adventure with commands. If you're new to using a CMD line (terminal) this is a perfect engaging way to become more familiar with how it works. Just like any new game once you get familiar with the controls you'll breeze through it. There is a clean graphic user interface that makes navigating the game environment (with your mouse) very intuitive. You are taught how to play in a standard tutorial so you're not just thrown out into the ocean expecting to be a 1337 h@ck0r. You will encounter several high and low points that will continue to test what you've learned. At no point in the game did I feel like it was repetitive. You will have time to become familiar with your tools and soon after your tools will grow, allowing you to tackle harder and more complex hacker challenges. 

2. Story
No spoilers. I can say that there is a story and that you will be highly involved with in. There is a lot of mysteries, and plenty of interesting characters to learn about. I should mention that each new play through of the game will have many events randomized. In addition the story continues in the DLC and that I found it totally worth it.

3. Graphics
I find the graphics to be a nice blend between modern techno sci-fi and retro website design. It's actually quite an interesting blend of styles that seems to work out well. I can safely say this [b]isn't[/b] just a game where you look into singular black box and type commands. 

4. Final Thoughts
It's good. I personally had some doubts but once I started playing I couldn't stop. I wouldn't be leaving a review if I didn't think it deserved more attention.

TL;DR - Be the best Hackerman you can be just for a few bucks. Don't missout and be a scriptkiddie like Newman on Jurassic Park, a dinosaur ate his face...don't let a dinosaur eat your face.

***UPDATE - I finally played the DLC "Labyrinths" and damn, Picking it it up is a must if your gonna play this game. It opens up so much more and shows you easily what a Hacknet 2 could be.

After playing a game like Mainlining, I felt i had a love for a new genre of game but that game specifically just didn't satisfy me enough, it was wayyy to easy. I needed to know what the next level up from there was. After looking around a bit I found several other Hacker-esk types of games but only 2 specifically called out to me, Uplink and Hacknet. While it seems definitively that Uplink is the top dog in this genres arena, I gotta admit i didn't want to step into something that might be too overwhelming for me, so I went with Hacknet; the game people say is its spiritual sequel.

Having played this game now on my 3rd play through 35hrs in(pre dlc) i gotta say i think im in love. This game just feels right in a lot of places as to what you would want from a game like this.

The story while Is short and leaves some questions unanswered. It definitely makes you feel like you are part of its world for the most part. The fact that the world is open enough to have hidden crevices/coves of information to find behind hacked emails and encrypted documents, well outside of whatever story or mission you are focused on is more than enough to feel like this is a fun sandbox to play in.

The Interface is pretty much the only graphics you get but even so it does the job. And since you can change the theme/layout later in the game, the preference is on you, they all look great to me though.

The Music is amazing (some of it feels as good as a Hotline Miami soundtrack), it's sometimes perfectly in the foreground at times syncing to what you have to deal with at the moment and other times its just softly in the background letting you focus on what you need to do next.

This game is so simple but ingenious once you dive into it. I would recommend anyone that don't mind a bit of reading and some critical thinking puzzles pick this up.

I picked up Hacknet while it was free on Humble, and I have to say, if I had the money to go back and buy it I'd do it a hundred times. Hacknet is a beautiful game with a satisfying story, and it's chock full of easter eggs and tiny details that make it feel like you're actually part of the digial world this all takes place in. The game feels alive; it feels like you're actually breaking into systems people use on a day to tay basis. You'll find personal documents, corporate memos, IRC logs, humurous writing assignments, and much more scattered around the different machines, making it feel like there's an actual world here.

Admittedly, Hacknet does dumb down the hacking a fair bit, making it feel more like you're in CSI rather than a real hackerman. But this is fine. It's a game, it's not meant to be hyperrealistic and super challenging to learn. It doesn't take years of training and a cybersecurity certificationton pick up Hacknet. Additionally, what Hacknet lacks in realism, it more than makes up for in terms of interesting and challenging missions. There's so much to do, so many interesting surprises, and a healthy balance of comedic contracts like stealing fried chicken recipies with some rather serious moral choices. And as if that wasn't enough, many of its missions left me on the edge of my seat, sighing in relief as I [i]barely[/i] hit the mark with merely seconds to spare.

To top it off, Hacknet features a brilliant OST that I just can't stop listening to. Every song was carefully chosen to match the current atmosphere in the game, and it certainly shows. It really feels like you're in a movie here; when that email comes in and the song changes, you [u]know[/u] it's about to go down. 

Overall, Hacknet (and its Labyrinths DLC, which I also highly recommend) is one of the best games I've played. It features a compelling story that will rope you in, even if you aren't its main character. It will play with your emotions quite beautifully, and leave you victorious yet bittersweet. It's such a fascinating, well-designed and well-written game, and it left me begging for more.

My name is Byte, and if you're reading this, buy this game.

It's a game, it's not meant to be hyperrealistic and super challenging to learn. It doesn't take years of training and a cybersecurity certificationton pick up Hacknet. Additionally, what Hacknet lacks in realism, it more than makes up for in terms of interesting and challenging missions. There's so much to do, so many interesting surprises, and a healthy balance of comedic contracts like stealing fried chicken recipies with some rather serious moral choices. And as if that wasn't enough, many of its missions left me on the edge of my seat, sighing in relief as I [i]barely[/i] hit the mark with merely seconds to spare. To top it off, Hacknet features a brilliant OST that I just can't stop listening to. Every song was carefully chosen to match the current atmosphere in the game, and it certainly shows. It really feels like you're in a movie here; when that email comes in and the song changes, you [u]know[/u] it's about to go down. Overall, Hacknet (and its Labyrinths DLC, which I also highly recommend) is one of the best games I've played. It features a compelling story that will rope you in, even if you aren't its main character. It will play with your emotions quite beautifully, and leave you victorious yet bittersweet. It's such a fascinating, well-designed and well-written game, and it left me begging for more. My name is Byte, and if you're reading this, buy this game.

[h1] An updated lite version of Uplink. [/h1]

Hacknet is amazing, but what keeps it from topping Uplink is that it has less features and flexibility. 

[b]Disclaimer: I've not yet completed the entire game. But based on a wild experience I've had with it, I felt prompted to write the review. [/b]

If you played Uplink, this is basically an updated version of the game.  Focused on command consoles, IP, file retrieval/removal all in a neat little interface.

It takes some of the very same queues from Uplink in its story, as you investigate about a hacker named Bit.

Pros:
[list]
[*]Authentic feel
[*]Challenging yet very satisfying
[*]Outstanding music
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
[*]No money system. The fun part of Uplink was going off on the side and robbing banks wirelessly, and using the money to build an unstoppable system, and simply feeling rewarded for your contracts.
[*]No hardware to upgrade. 
[*]Tutorials and in-game info isn't always clear. I know its not supposed to hand-hold. But it feels like many commands are left out, as well as some contracts aren't clear about what they want sometimes. The explanation of Shells and Trapping are complete garbage. That needs to be fixed. 
[*]Lack of freedom. Uplink had a lot more freedom in becoming a white hat, black hat, or grey hat.  Also had more in the way of non-linear gameplay choices. 
[*]Lack of freedom in file editing. In uplink you could change log files, and put someone elses IP in place of your own... Leading to hilarious results as you pin your hacks on someone else. 
[/list]

[b][u]What's awesome:[/u][/b] Unlike Uplink, it gives you a chance at redemption if you fail some missings, and even a chance at revenge. 

[b][u]What's not awesome:[/u][/b] The very linear gameplay.

[b][u]One major letdown [/u][/b]: No sandbox mode/options. 

[b]Overall: Some glaring bad decisions aside, it is a great game. It tense, it makes you feel like a hacker, it has some great polish, and all this for the price its asking is a no brainer. It's a very decent game, but it COULD have been great.  Still waiting for the real Uplink 2 to stand up. [/b]

Wow.... this game was amazing.... Just finished and am in that state of almost shock you feel after finishing a fantastic book or tv series. Wow.

I'll start with the negatives: to be honest, in the middle, the game gets slightly (and I do mean slightly) redundant. You do the same things to hack into a server or computer, you find what you're looking for, get out, and complete your contract. But that's really only for the contracts during the middle of the game. When you get into more complicated missions, finding hidden servers and connected devices, everything becomes much more interesting. The repetition never made me feel bored or want to stop playing. 

Also, the game was a bit short. I felt like it could've used more missions and more story, but I'm not sure there was room for that without making the game ACTUALLY feel repetitive, so no problem there. Also, it'll take up as much of your time as you would expect of a $10 (for $7 if you got it on sale like I did) game. 

But these two problems are not at all enough to keep me from recommending this game to others. The story is really engaging, the puzzles are interesting and rewarding (not too straightforward while also not being impossible), and the music and style of the game is on point. If you come from a programming background (specifically using the linux command line), you'll probably be disappointed that this perfectly realistic, but it's obviously not meant to be. It makes you feel like a hacker, it's not an educational tool.

My point is that is game is amazing. This was both my first hacking and text based game, and I still loved it. Please do yourself a favor and play it. 10/10.

Note: I never had any game breaking bugs like many of the negative reviews reported. There were some things that worried me, like aborting a story mission and not knowing if I could pick it up again, but after a quick google search it appeared finishing the mission I aborted for made the mission "spawn" again, so everything was fine.

I’ve never hacked real computer systems (or anything for that matter), so take this statement with a grain of salt. Hacknet made me feel like a real hacker. A good game should be fun and immersive. Hacknet aces both of those criteria. The story starts you off getting an email from a hacker named ‘Bit’ who confesses to already being dead and needing your help to stop something horrible from coming.

The game does a good job of introducing itself. The mechanic is based mostly in a terminal prompt with a retro-esque UI. The number of commands that you need to remember are minimal thankfully and most of the navigating to do routine tasks can be done by simply clicking. However, if you’re looking for a purer feeling everything can be done purely from command line. The parts of the game that require breaking into a computer system do require use of the command line for the most part.

Once you have the basics of breaking into a system down, the game then raises the difficulty by introducing a system where you are traced by the system you are trying to break into. While the steps of hacking don’t change much as the game progresses, the game does make sure to include new challenges. Make sure you have pen and paper nearby, there is plenty you will need to write down. (Or take pictures with your phone like I did) As the game continues, the challenges become less about breaking into the system itself and more about following a trail of information to get what you need. This includes thinking about the information given rather than simply following instructions. 

I won’t say that the game is without flaw. In a few places what you need to do to complete a task takes more than just normal careful consideration. I am fully willing to accept lack of intelligence on my part as the excuse for this. 

In short, if you like puzzle games and you’re not put off by my description, then do give this game a chance. The experience is well worth the price.

Late review, but, just gonna say: Awesome game.

Great Soundtrack, Colorful UI, Amazing Mechanics and somewhat Touching Story.

I would say something about each part, but really, words can't exactly describe the neat feeling of Hacking to a beat from the likes of Remi Gallego, Carpenter Brut, Tonspender and much more.

Being a computer geek personally, I can verify the whole 'Based on real UNIX commands' thing is pretty spot on. Granted, it removes a few commands, but I am sure that can be passed on given the audience this is meant for (All.)

I highly recommend this game if you're a little tired of something like 'Uplink' for instance. Or if you just generally want to feel like a Hacker. It's really addicting.

9.8/10

Now, honestly, this sort of lacks a few things though, and they might be commonly shared things. Like... Upgrades, as one thing. It's understandable to not add Upgrades, since it would probably make the player OP. But really, it would be nice to get additional RAM throughout the game. I don't exactly care how, or why, it just seems like something that would be a good addition. Another thing could also be more Paths. This is a bit of a spoiler, so read off from this next bit if you haven't unlocked all the achievements or done everything possible:

So far, I only found 2 paths to go on. The first path being the goody-two-shoes, going with Entropy, and going through with the CSEC tests. The second path being tracking Naix, deleting his files, and then going on from his E-Mail to vandalize Nortron's servers, to get into the /el community (A really funny spoof to the likes of 4 Chan, 8Chan, or any particular Image Board that stays in the theme of Free-Speech.) and going on from there. Personally, I would love to see something like a 'Independant' path or a 'Brutal' path. Something like those I wish could be in this.

But, asides from all this though, again, really awesome game.

Side Note: Red Line. Have fun with that ;)

review_text_raw: Ever want to be a Hacker? or at least pretend ? Well in Hacknet, its an immersive hacking terminal based simulator. Trust me it looks and feels pretty legit. If it wasn't for the ambient music in the background, sometimes you do feel like your well, hacking.  Start with making a profile and then a tutorial, to learn the ins and the outs of how to get into someones computer then probe, scan and do whatever to the files as you want/need. Then from there, work on contracts or jobs to boost your reputation to gain entry into some pretty hardcore hacker groups like Entropy and CSEC. These open up harder contracts and jobs and progresses the story line of the game. The game bases on you learning and memorizing what to do as you go along to get faster. It's all about punching in the right programming codes into the terminal at the right time.  Yes, typing is the game. Some contracts and jobs are rather well written and clever, so reading is suggested while hacking other peoples computers. Some jobs seem like viable legit reasons why there are hackers. Not all the jobs are for nefarious reasons. Arch- Nemesis? WHY YES ,THERE IS ONE! It does great to the story line. I suggest that when you get hacked yourself, it may look very very real and if you have really immersed yourself into the game, you might freak and turn your computer off. Remember behind every spy and secret agent, there's that computer techie that knows his stuff and gets them through the day. That's you. The game is rather straight forward graphics of terminal, colored windows and ambient music. Not an action game. There is a fun lil clicker game, within the game you can hack into, if that's your thing.

I enjoyed this experience. Good that I bought it.

There's only one problem: Typos?

Okay, so now for the real review:

HACKNET is a game about hacking in a simplified way. You launch your virtual mashine and recieve the message of a dead-man's trigger program from a Hacker who may have died (that's why it's called Dead-man's trigger). The program will give you a fast tutorial about the gameplay, which appears to be like linux terminal based hacking and launching programs you have stolen to crack security measures so you can take control of other virtual maschines, read their data, steal their data and then cover up your trails. review_text_raw:
I have played through this game 4 times now, and still find other ways to solve things and find little secrets.

This is the very first completely text-based story game to get me hooked, and oh boy has it got me hooked.
the puzzles this game challenges you to solve are very smartly set up, in the later stages of the game you really feel like you are the one digging all the stuff up, not like the game gives you the pieces of information you need.

The story itself is interesting, but nothing out of the ordinary to be honest. What's so special is that every mission you do has it's own amusing, sad, or interesting story to it. This makes the playthrough feel like some sort of book, where you read the experiences of different characters which are all different to one and another, but all stories play into the main soryline. 
Especially missions like Junebug or Naix really help to sell the story of you being a hacker doing all of this from your own PC, you will know what I am talking about when you have played this game, what you should definately do in my opinion.

Overall is this one of my favourite games, ranking in my top 5 for sure, worth every cent of the 10 bucks.
